metadata.document_title: Clinical Practice Overview: Appendicitis Symptoms, Diagnosis, and Surgical/Antibiotic Management

sections.text: Symptoms of appendicitis typically begin with a dull aching pain in the middle of the abdomen (tummy) around the navel (belly button). Over a period of several hours, the pain characteristically moves to the lower right side of the abdomen (the right iliac fossa / McBurney's point) and progressively worsens. The pain is aggravated by movement, coughing, walking, or pressing on the area. Other common clinical symptoms include nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite (anorexia), low-grade pyrexia (fever), constipation or diarrhea, and urinary frequency. If appendicitis is not treated promptly, the inflamed appendix can perforate or burst, leading to temporary sudden relief of pain followed rapidly by severe, generalized peritonitis across the entire abdomen.

Appendicitis is diagnosed through comprehensive clinical physical examination, laboratory testing, and diagnostic imaging. Physical examination involves abdominal palpation assessing for localized tenderness, rebound tenderness, and involuntary guarding in the right lower quadrant. Diagnostic investigations include complete blood counts to evaluate elevated white blood cell counts (leukocytosis), C-reactive protein (CRP) inflammatory markers, urinalysis to exclude urinary tract infection, and pregnancy testing for females of reproductive age to exclude ectopic pregnancy. Imaging modalities include abdominal ultrasound scans (frequently first-line in children and pregnant women) and contrast-enhanced CT scans to confirm luminal appendiceal dilation, wall thickening, and peri-appendiceal fat stranding.

The definitive standard treatment for acute appendicitis is surgical removal of the appendix, termed an appendectomy. An appendectomy is performed as an urgent or emergency operation under general anesthesia. Laparoscopic (keyhole) surgery is the preferred approach, utilizing 3 small incisions through which a laparoscope and surgical instruments are inserted to dissect and ligate the appendix at its base with minimal tissue disruption. Open surgery involves a single larger transverse or oblique incision (e.g., McBurney or Rocky-Davis incision) in the lower right abdomen, which is indicated when the appendix has perforated, an extensive abscess is present, severe peritoneal contamination exists, or prior abdominal adhesions prevent safe laparoscopic visual access.

sections.section_title: Conservative Antibiotic Therapy and Appendix Mass Management
sections.text: In select patients with uncomplicated acute appendicitis without evidence of perforation, abscess, or appendicolith, conservative antibiotic management may be considered as an alternative when surgery presents high anesthetic or operative risk. Conservative protocol involves intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics followed by a full course of oral antibiotics with close hospital monitoring. Furthermore, when appendiceal inflammation leads to adherence of adjacent omentum and bowel loops forming an inflammatory phlegmon termed an 'appendix mass', initial treatment is non-operative intravenous antibiotic therapy. An interval appendectomy may subsequently be evaluated several weeks after the acute inflammatory phlegmon has resolved.

Appendiceal perforation represents a surgical emergency leading to peritonitis and sepsis. Emergency red flags requiring immediate hospital transfer or emergency service dispatch include: sudden extreme worsening of abdominal pain, abdominal wall rigidity ('board-like abdomen'), persistent high fever, rapid heart rate (tachycardia), rapid breathing, confusion, and pale, blotchy skin indicating systemic septic shock. Patients should not ingest food, liquids, or oral laxatives before medical assessment, as laxatives increase intraluminal pressure and heighten the risk of appendiceal rupture.
